Greek Automotive Industry Faces Severe Credit Freeze as Companies Struggle to Secure Financing

A sudden credit freeze has gripped Greece’s automotive industry, leaving vehicle importers and dealerships struggling to secure vital financing. The situation, triggered by a sharp tightening of lending criteria among Greek banks this month, has resulted in delayed shipments, slumping sales, and growing uncertainty across the sector.

Cars Motorcycles and Marine Engine Trade and Import Co SA, a leading importer and distributor, confirmed it has been unable to access working capital for nearly two weeks. “We are facing delays in unloading new vehicles at the port of Piraeus because we cannot settle payments with suppliers,” said Christos Demetriou, the company’s chief financial officer. “If this continues, we will be forced to furlough staff and postpone all new orders.”

The Hellenic Association of Automotive Importers estimates that passenger car deliveries in June have dropped by 38% compared to May, while new vehicle registrations are expected to fall to a three-year low. “The entire industry is on edge. Financing for both inventory and consumer purchases has dried up overnight,” said Eleni Papadopoulou, spokesperson for the association.

Smaller firms, such as Aegean Auto Traders Ltd, have reported difficulty obtaining even short-term credit lines, with several dealerships warning of imminent liquidity shortages. “We are seeing sales contracts cancelled because buyers cannot get auto loans approved,” said Giorgos Kotsakis, owner of a central Athens dealership.

Employees’ union representatives have called for urgent government intervention to stabilize credit flows and protect jobs. “Without immediate action, we risk a wave of layoffs in the coming weeks,” warned Vassilis Markakis, head of the union representing automotive retail workers.

At the time of writing, talks between industry leaders and government officials are ongoing, but no concrete measures have yet been announced.
